The median here is $1,202 a year (single-family primary home, premium plus fees, in force August 31, 2026). That is 2% below the New Jersey median of $1,231 and 13% above the U.S. median of $1,066. It is 7th lowest of 21 New Jersey counties with 100+ priced policies.

By ZIP (the 38 with 25+ priced policies), the median ranges from $702 (07755 Oakhurst) to $1,747 (07748).

This year’s bills: policies whose term began Jan–Aug 2026 (renewals and policies sold this year together) typically pay $1,237. Buying? Policies first bought in the past year typically pay $1,291. Why prices differ.

Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

66.9% of Monmouth County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones. That is a share of insured policy units, not of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 12.3% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE.

Flood map: FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Monmouth County has 123 map panels, the oldest in effect since September 25, 2009 and the newest since June 15, 2022. FEMA has revised that map by 5 Letters of Map Revision, 1 of them in effect since January 1, 2021.

Owners here asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone 840 times (rulings in FEMA's LOMA map layer):

  • 597 took the building or some or all of the lot out
  • 93 found it already outside the zone as mapped
  • 100 were denied
  • 50 were other or mixed

FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one.

These counts are for owners who applied, not your home's odds. FEMA's map service gives no dates for them. They are counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here.

FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

Flood insurance cost in Monmouth County, New Jersey

In Monmouth County, single-family primary-home NFIP policies typically cost about $1,202 a year ($100 a month), fees included. Half pay between $872 and $1,682. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $872 · Typical $1,202 · A quarter pay over $1,682 · A tenth pay $2,077 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 9,958 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: find it in the NAIC's directory of state insurance departments.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Monmouth County, New Jersey: what floods pay out

Floods in Monmouth County have led to 19,597 NFIP flood claims and $896.0 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 1992 and 2011.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($779,687,679), 1992 ($53,977,947), 2011 ($27,753,411). Total paid $896,001,706. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: 445 claims here from losses 2016–2025 have a flood zone on the claim. Of these, 39.6% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D). They got 32.7% of the dollars paid on these claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Most do: 86.3% of claims in Monmouth County paid something. The average paid claim was $55,312 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 43.5% of the 7,280 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 7,280 policies reporting one)43.5%New Jersey: 38.1%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)86.0%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 16,448 claims paid with a damage figure)3.7%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? The premium is based on the flood risk of the building. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How Monmouth County appears in the national research papers

Each paper sorts the U.S. counties with enough records by one measure into five groups of about equal size, from highest fifth to lowest fifth. A group is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: Of 201 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage here (losses 2016–2025), 0.5% (90% range 0.1–2.2%) had recorded building damage over the building coverage. That ranks in the lowest fifth of 268 U.S. counties listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: Of 337 claims with a payment and a rated zone here (losses 2016–2025), 40.7% (90% range 36.3–45.1%) were rated outside zones A and V. That ranks in the second-highest fifth of 364 U.S. counties listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 9,914 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible here, 15.1% (90% range 14.5–15.7%) had a building deductible of $5,000 or more on record. That ranks in the second-lowest fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: Of 445 NFIP claims with a month of loss here (losses 2016–2025), 33.9% (90% range 30.3–37.7%) were in their county's peak month. That ranks in the lowest fifth of 416 U.S. counties listed. Peak month: September, over half of it from September 2023 alone. At random, 10.6% of claims would land in one month at this size, so the ranking uses the share above that.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 9,958 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways here, 44.5% (90% range 43.7–45.3%) had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium. That ranks in the second-highest fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for coastal flooding and Relatively High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience. It is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. FEMA's model puts yearly flood loss here at roughly $7.6 million for coastal flooding and $109.6 million for inland flooding. It counts buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not, so it runs far above insurance payouts. A separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value, is higher here than in about 79% of U.S. counties for coastal flooding and about 29% for inland flooding. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Local sea level: NOAA's tide gauge at Sandy Hook measured a sea-level trend of +1.68 inches per decade (give or take 0.04) from 1932 to 2025. A plus sign means the water there got higher over that period. A tide gauge measures one spot on the coast; it is not your property's flood risk.

Source: NOAA Tides & Currents — Sea Level Trends. Data: NOAA's published trends; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $78.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,674 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.
